A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiffVax, with matching authors, core methodology and retained experiments. The main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original image and video experiments, loss ablations, prompt-generalization experiments and a 67-participant user study.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds comparisons and experiments concerning sampling settings, perturbation budgets, counter-attacks, model transfer and mask variation.

M1.justification: Both versions use UNet++ to generate masked additive perturbations, clamp the immunized image, and train with the same noise and editing losses before single-pass inference. v2 expands the inference explanation and documents mask-free editing; its alternative-norm experiments do not establish a change to the default method.

E1.justification: v2 expands the evaluated content and attack scenarios to include artistic transformations of artwork, multiple-object manipulations, mismatched or partial editing masks, and IMPRESS purification (Figure 6; Appendices A.2.3, A.3.3 and A.4.3). Human images, non-human subjects, videos and InstructPix2Pix editing already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: DiffusionGuard becomes an evaluated comparator in the principal image comparison, counter-attack experiments and video evaluation: v1 Tables 2, 5 and 3 correspond to v2 Tables 1, 2 and 11. This substantially expands competitive validation beyond the retained Random Noise and PhotoGuard comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled sampling-step and sampler comparisons, fixed baseline perturbation budgets, multiple JPEG strengths and SD v1.5-to-v2 transfer protocols. It also expands metrics in video, counter-attack and ablation evaluations. Section 4 now describes 875 images with 800 training and 75 testing images, while Appendix A.1 retains v1's 1,000-image, 80/20 account; this inconsistency does not establish that the underlying split changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss-component, loss-weight and prompt-generalization studies, v2 adds analyses of sampling settings, perturbation budgets, stronger counter-attacks, model transfer, mask mismatch and alternative loss norms. Training curves and explicit failure cases involving small objects, extreme mask differences and visible perturbations further expand the analysis (Appendices A.1–A.8).

E5.justification: The three image-specific training setups and distributions over 75 seen and 75 unseen prompts are retained from v1 Section S.3/Figure 6 in v2 Appendix A.6/Figure 20. v2 adds no seed reporting, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or formal significance tests; the new averaged training curves do not change this practice.

E6.justification: Reported DiffVax seen/unseen SSIM changes from 0.519/0.534 to 0.510/0.526, and CLIP-T from 26.67/26.74 to 23.13/24.17 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). Video PSNR changes from 14.54 to 16.78 (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 11). Numerous comparator, robustness and transfer results are added. These are revised reported outcomes, without sufficient explanation to attribute them to a controlled performance improvement; user-study rankings and loss-weight results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The diffusion preliminaries, perturbation formulation and training equations retain their mathematical substance. v2 writes the noise-loss norm using p but explicitly selects p = 1, matching v1. Its discussions of learnability and perturbation frequency introduce no formal theorem, proof or derivation.

C1.justification: The central efficiency and image/video protection claims remain, but v2 Section 5 broadens the claimed generalization to unseen editing-model versions and mismatched masks, and asserts a learnable structure of effective perturbations. v1 emphasized unseen-content generalization and separately trained editing tools. v2 still acknowledges model specificity while claiming substantially broader transfer capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 newly attributes robustness to spatially targeted, low-frequency perturbations and interprets generalization as evidence of learnable perturbation structure. It substantially expands the earlier per-tool limitation with concrete failures involving multiple small objects, extreme mask mismatch and perceptible noise, plus qualifications concerning architectural transfer and temporal modeling (Appendices A.4–A.9).

D1.justification: The principal training details, including UNet++, Adam, 350 epochs, batch size 5, A100 hardware and approximately 22 hours, were already supplied in v1. v2 adds mask-free loss handling, JPEG-strength disclosure, participant instructions and randomized presentation details. It also states that source code and reproduction guidelines are supplied in supplementary materials and adds a CCP dataset access reference.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion expands substantially to cover DiffusionGuard, PCA, EditShield, pixel-domain attacks, Mist, AdvDM, SDS and generative adversarial perturbations. Appendices A.2.2 and A.2.4 additionally explain comparison exclusions and position evaluation coverage against other immunization work. These changes extend research positioning beyond bibliographic or citation-style updates.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, methodology and experimental narrative, adds a distinct inference explanation, and replaces the short conclusion with a broader discussion. Implementation details, the algorithm and video evaluation move to a reorganized appendix with a contents page and dedicated discussion, limitations and reproducibility sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. v2 adds a comparison schematic, redraws the method diagram to distinguish training and inference, restructures and expands comparison tables, and adds training, transfer, mask, norm and failure-case displays. Retained material is also relocated, including the user-study rankings and prompt-distribution plot.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the paper's robustness and generalization claims. DiffusionGuard comparisons, controlled attack-setting studies, direct transfer tests and illustrated failure cases address important gaps in v1's narrower validation. Expanded related work and explicit applicability limits also improve assessability. These gains are tempered by inconsistent 875-versus-1,000-image accounts, conflicting low- versus high-frequency perturbation descriptions, and unexplained revisions to existing scores. Those reporting weaknesses limit interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical scrutiny and disclosure of failures.
